extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy (readers of introductory/advanced logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and classify the kinds of propositions, the ontology of predicates/attributes (essential vs accidental), and the logical doctrine of predicables (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens). Shows how abstract terms map to concrete terms and how propositions function in reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five fundamental kinds of matter asserted in propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: All (non-verbal) propositions assert one of five things: Existence, Order in Place, Order in Time (Sequence/Co-existence), Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing any substantive proposition, identify which of these five it affirms or denies. This classification underpins what is susceptible of proof and what kind of evidence or reasoning is appropriate (e.g., causal claims require causal evidence; resemblance claims are about similarity of phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Order in Place and Co-inherence/Co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Order in Place concerns arrangement in space (positional/locational relations); Co-inherence (a species of co-existence) denotes the concurrence of two or more attributes or powers in the same part/locality (e.g., weight, color, lustre in gold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate spatial order with co-inherence of attributes. Co-inherence is often temporal/simultaneous (belongs to Time as part of simultaneity) and may be potential rather than actual (e.g., 'snow is white' even in darkness because whiteness would be perceived when light returns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract terms map to concrete terms (transformability principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposition formed with abstract terms can be transformed into a precisely equivalent proposition using concrete terms — either concrete names that connote the attributes or the facts/phenomena (fundamenta) grounding those attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or clarifying an abstract proposition, render it in concrete terms (e.g., 'Thoughtlessness is dangerous' → 'Thoughtless actions are dangerous') to expose the actual fact-type asserted (existence, sequence, causation, etc.). This aids analysis and evidential assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes denote one of the five kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: An attribute (or combination of attributes) must, in predicate use, amount to either an Existence, a Co-existence, a Causation, a Sequence, or a Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a predicate is an abstract name (an attribute), interpret claims about it as asserting one of these five relations about the phenomena or facts that ground the attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential versus actual presence of attributes (epistemic potentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attribute may be considered as in existence even when the grounding fact is not presently actual but only potentially present (e.g., whiteness of snow in darkness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for potential or latent states when judging whether co-inherence/co-existence is asserted; this affects whether a proposition claims current perception or dispositional/potential properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions merely verbal: propositions about meanings/usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions relate only to the meanings of names (verbal/merely verbal propositions) and so are not strictly susceptible to truth or falsity but only to conformity with usage or convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such propositions as matters for proof of linguistic usage (showing words have been used in the asserted sense) rather than empirical proof. They occupy an important place in logic but differ in kind from factual propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential (verbal) versus accidental (real) propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential propositions predicate attributes that are already connoted by the name (they unfold the meaning of the name and give no new factual information). Accidental (non-essential or real) propositions predicate attributes not involved in the subject's signification and therefore convey substantive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'essential' propositions function largely as definitions or verbal clarifications; substantive reasoning and informative claims are the accidental/real propositions. When evaluating arguments, prioritize non-essential claims for evidential scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit assumption of existence in essential propositions used for demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: When essential propositions appear to yield important consequences (e.g., in mathematics), this is typically because there is an implicit assumption that the named objects really exist; without assuming existence, essential predication alone yields no empirical consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to hidden existential assumptions when deriving consequences from definitional claims; make existential premises explicit before treating such inferences as factual demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should unfold connotation (completeness vs pragmatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete definition should unfold the whole connotation of a name (when connotative), though in practice definitions commonly specify only enough attributes to mark out the usual objects denoted; sometimes accidental properties are used for convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rigorous analysis, prefer definitions that state the full connotation; for practical classification or communication, a narrower set of identifying attributes may be acceptable. Note the difference when assessing precision of claims or definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper role of propositions in reasoning: propositions as marks/evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides expressing theoretical relations (e.g., 'attributes of man are accompanied by mortality'), propositions have a practical use: as memoranda or marks indicating what to expect in individual cases — i.e., that one fact is evidence or a mark of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reasoning and argument construction, adopt the 'mark/evidence' perspective to show how a general proposition helps infer or warrant belief about particular instances; this view is especially useful in forming premises for inductive or abductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using essential propositions as primary examples in teaching logic (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples used historically in elementary logic (e.g., 'Every man is rational') are often essential propositions that add no informational content beyond word meaning, and thus misrepresent the usefulness of syllogistic methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing pedagogical examples or evaluating logical arguments, prefer non-trivial, non-essential propositions that genuinely require proof or reasoning, so as not to create the impression that logical methods are vacuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicables — fivefold taxonomy of predicate relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Predicates may be classified by their relation to the subject on a given occasion into Genus, Species, Differentia, Proprium, and Accidens (the Predicables). This classification depends on the class denoted and the subject, not on fixed meanings of names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a predicate, determine which predicable it exemplifies relative to the subject (e.g., 'animal' is a genus relative to 'man' but a species relative to 'substance'). Use this to clarify hierarchical and relational structure in classification and definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of genus/species/differentia to context
rubrics_metrics.description: A given name can function as genus, species, differentia, or accident depending on the subject and the classification context (e.g., 'rectangular' is a differentia of square but an accident of a table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate predicates contextually; avoid reifying labels as inherently 'genus' or 'species'—their predicable status is relative and should be determined in each classificatory instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predication vs. classification: attributes vs class membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Predication asserts attributes (what the name connotes) and does not presuppose classification, although the act of introducing a general name creates a class if objects correspond to the signification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critique or construction of propositions, focus on the attributes connoted rather than treating class-membership as primary. Recognize that names sometimes arise from classificatory convenience rather than prior ontological groupings.
